research_domain_title: Human Capital Infrastructure, Pathways, and Regional Academies
note: Major doctrine and website architecture. Regional academies are one possible institutional model to research and pilot — not a locked statewide design. No invented enrollment, retention, or earnings statistics. ASMSA is noted as an institutional reference for residential public academies, not a sourced outcome evaluation in this slice.
role_in_philosophy: Human capital infrastructure fits rural strength, productive capacity, geographic opportunity, local leadership, ownership, families, and education connected to community needs. Prosperity grows when every person's talents are developed and connected to the needs of their communities.

human_capital_infrastructure.summary: Societies already build highways, bridges, broadband, and water systems. Constitutional Capitalism argues that a state should also deliberately build human infrastructure — institutions whose primary purpose is producing capable, healthy, innovative citizens.

first_principle.text: Every child should graduate with a meaningful pathway to productive adulthood. A constitutional republic should intentionally cultivate the talents of every citizen by providing multiple respected pathways—including skilled trades, entrepreneurship, higher education, public service, agriculture, manufacturing, healthcare, technology, and the arts—rather than assuming a single model of success.

equal_dignity_rule.text: Present academies and other pathways as additional pathways of equal dignity — not as alternatives that demote traditional education. Welding, nursing, software, farming, electrical work, teaching, and engineering all contribute essential skills to building strong communities.

pilot_posture.rule: Present regional academies as one possible institutional model to be researched and piloted, rather than assuming a single statewide design before testing.
pilot_posture.portable_doctrine: The Human Capital Doctrine is broad enough to adapt across states and countries; Arkansas may become an early demonstration site through regional academies.

arkansas_academy_model.naming_rule: The name should communicate engines of regional development — not merely vocational schools. Trades are essential; so are entrepreneurship, technology, healthcare, public administration, engineering, conservation, and emergency services.
arkansas_academy_model.mission: To prepare young Arkansans to build prosperous lives in the communities they call home by combining academic excellence, technical mastery, civic leadership, entrepreneurship, and real-world experience.
arkansas_academy_model.mission_note: The mission is about making home stronger — not about leaving home.

living_learning_campus.summary: Students could live, study, intern, build businesses, serve communities, and graduate with industry credentials, apprenticeships, college credit, business plans, savings, professional networks, and civic experience.

institutional_reference.name: Arkansas School for Mathematics, Sciences, and the Arts
institutional_reference.role: Interesting institutional reference showing Arkansas can operate a public residential academy serving students from across the state.
institutional_reference.limit: Not treated here as a sourced outcome evaluation; the proposal extends the residential-academy concept into regional workforce and community development.

regional_specialization.rule: Instead of every academy teaching everything, each region develops excellence around its economy. Students may still attend academies outside their home region when interests align.
regional_specialization.note: Illustrative regional examples for design discussion — not a locked map or inventory of existing programs.

paid_apprenticeships.rule: Every student should graduate having worked — real employers, real wages, real mentors — not only simulated work.

entrepreneurship.rule: Entrepreneurship should be equal in importance to trades.
entrepreneurship.aspiration: Imagine graduating high school already capable of launching a viable enterprise.

civic_leadership.rule: Produce future citizens ready to lead, not only workers ready to be hired.

community_partnerships.purpose: Keep curriculum connected to real community needs.

beyond_graduation_rates: graduates employed in their chosen field
graduates remaining in or returning to Arkansas
success_metrics.alignment: Measure human flourishing, not only institutional performance.
success_metrics.note: Metric agenda only — no invented values.

human_capital_test.title: Human Capital Test
human_capital_test.purpose: Screen education and human-infrastructure proposals before acceptance into the framework.

questions.text: Does it give every child a meaningful pathway to productive adulthood?
Does it treat skilled trades, entrepreneurship, higher education, public service, and the arts as pathways of equal dignity?
Does it strengthen the communities students call home rather than treating departure as the default measure of success?
Is curriculum connected to real regional economic and civic needs?
Does it include real work with real wages and mentors, not only simulated experience?
Does entrepreneurship receive equal seriousness alongside technical training?
Does it prepare students for civic leadership as well as employment?
Are employers, local governments, educators, and community institutions partners in design and accountability?
Are success metrics focused on flourishing — employment, ownership, civic participation, and community strength — not only graduation rates?
Is the model proposed as a researchable pilot rather than an untested statewide lock-in?

research_status.next: Phase 2.1: register education/workforce primary sources; design pilot evaluation protocol for regional academies without inventing outcomes; keep ASMSA as institutional reference until sourced evaluation exists
